newsitem.title: USA: Internet startup targets Web advertising mart.
newsitem.headline: Internet startup targets Web advertising mart.

text.p: An Internet startup company will unveil an advertising transaction system it hopes will create a new market for placing and pricing of Internet ads in real-time, company executives said.

In interviews ahead of Monday's announcement, executives of fledgling FlyCast Communications said they expect next month to begin deploying a system that would allow each ad impression to be priced in a nearly real-time transaction.

Utilizing the Internet's unique ability to collect information about a specific viewer's profile, and by combining this with an advertiser's objectives and the context of a particular Web site, San Francisco-based FlyCast can enable variable price matching.

By using instant measurement techniques and FlyCast's AdAgent software to change advertising placement parameters on the fly, the company hopes to attract a major portion of the fast-growing Internet advertising space.

"This is a new way of buying and selling and establishing market leadership," said Larry Braitman, vice president of marketing at FlyCast. "Right now the cost of sales are too high and the revenues are too low (in Internet advertising)."

Massachusetts-based Forrester Research projects total Internet advertising spending will rise from $400 million this year to nearly $4.8 billion in the year 2000, more than 10-fold growth, although still only a small percentage of worldwide advertising spend.

Nonetheless, FlyCast faces a difficult challenge in lining up Web sites, content providers and advertisers behind a new model that differs from the advertising industry's traditional media buying practices, some analysts said.

"This captures our imagination, because the Net makes it more possible than elsewhere, but the fact remains that real-time markets don't really exist so far," said Bill Doyle, senior analyst for media and technology at Forrester.

Doyle estimates that in 1996, Web sites with advertising as a whole sold only 15 percent of available inventory, a sign there could be a tremendous market for a company that could match advertisers with vacant advertising space.
He said other groups had worked with Internet advertising barter and the concept of a real-time media auction, but that it has not yet been demonstrated the market will support such a model.

To succeed, FlyCast may need to work with existing advertising networks, such as those run by Infoseek and by DoubleClick (http://www.doubclick.net), which has a system to track use of banner advertisements.
Meanwhile, some Web sites like (http://junkbusters.com) offer to help Web surfers block out advertising, an activity that could diminish the use of Internet advertising overall.

Advertisers and content providers receive instant feedback on individual target viewers on various Web sites, enabling higher value impressions than currently delivered from specific locations on a generic pricing structure.

FlyCast is completing a technical trial of its service and says it has signed up leading interactive advertising agencies, including J. Walter Thompson, BBDO, SiteSpecific Inc., and Fallon McElligott, for its initial deployment.

Agency executives were not available for comment, but Thomas Gewecke, publisher of online services at PC World Communications, Inc., a participating Internet on-line publisher, said creation of a spot market for Web ads could boost efficiency and return on investment.

Under its business model, FlyCast will receive a portion of the transaction cost and initially will charge a nominal fee per agent for advertisers to sign up. FlyCast's Web site is (http://www.flycast.com).
